title: Race conditions: when timing decides the answer
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why counter++ is not one operation, produce a race you can measure, and use a tool that finds races your test run happened not to trigger.

blocks.text: A race condition is a program whose result depends on which thread got there first. The frightening part is not that the answer is wrong — it is that the answer is usually right. A race that corrupts one value in ten thousand passes every test you will write by hand.

blocks.caption: One line of C, three machine steps
lines: /*   1. load  counter from memory into a register */
/*   3. store the register back to memory         */
/*   Thread B: load 5     <- reads before A stored              */
/* Two increments happened. The counter went up by one.         */

blocks.text: Eight threads each incrementing an unsynchronised counter 200,000 times should reach 1,600,000. On one 10-core machine, three consecutive runs produced 424,919 — 316,653 — 364,760. That is not a rounding error. Roughly three-quarters of all the increments vanished, and the amount lost was different every time.

blocks.title: The result that should worry you most
blocks.text: Compiled with -O2 instead of -O0, the same program printed exactly 1,600,000 on every run. It was not correct — the optimiser had noticed that the loop's only effect was to add 200,000 to a variable, and replaced 200,000 separate increments with a single add. One load, one add, one store: too fast to interleave. The bug was still there; the window had closed. This is why 'I tested it and the number was right' is not evidence that concurrent code is correct.

items: Any read-modify-write of shared data: counters, totals, reference counts
Check-then-act: 'if the key is absent, insert it' — another thread can insert between the two steps
Lazy initialisation: two threads both find the object missing and both create one
Linked structures: two threads appending to a list can lose an item or build a cycle
Files and paths: check that a file does not exist, then create it — the classic security race in the last module of this course

blocks.text: Note that only the first involves a counter. The general shape is: two steps that must not be separated, with nothing preventing separation.
The tool that does not depend on luck

Thread sanitizer instruments memory accesses and reports two threads touching the same location without synchronisation — even when the run happened to produce the right answer. It is the same family of tool as the address sanitizer from the C course, and it belongs in the same place: your normal build during development.

blocks.caption: Finding a race that did not misbehave
lines: #   Read of size 8 at 0x... by thread T2:
#   Previous write of size 8 at 0x... by thread T1:
# SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: data race race.c:13 in bump
1600000 / 1600000        <- and the total was CORRECT this run
# It named the line, both threads, and the variable — on a run

blocks.title: Two practical notes
blocks.text: Thread sanitizer slows a program down by roughly an order of magnitude and increases memory use substantially, so it is a development and CI tool, not a production one. It cannot be combined with address sanitizer in one build — run two builds when you want both. And inside a container you may need to relax the default seccomp profile (for example docker run --security-opt seccomp=unconfined), or the sanitizer aborts at startup with a CHECK failure about address randomisation.

rows: volatile controls compiler optimisation and reordering; load-add-store is still three steps. Measured at -O2 with volatile: 352,482 / 410,274 / 317,944 out of 1,600,000 — and note that adding volatile made the bug VISIBLE again at -O2 by preventing the loop collapse, without fixing anything
There is no size at which read-modify-write becomes one step
Changes the timing, does not remove the window
A race that fires rarely will pass a great many tests

blocks.text: The actual fixes are to make the sequence indivisible — a mutex, which the next lesson covers — or to use an atomic type, where the hardware guarantees the read-modify-write completes as one unit.

blocks.title: Produce the race, hide it, then find it anyway
steps: Write the eight-thread counter program: each thread does counter++ 200,000 times
Build with: gcc -O0 -pthread race.c -o race     and run it five times
Record the five totals — none should reach 1,600,000, and none should match each other
Now build with -O2 and run five times: the total is exactly right every time
Look at why: gcc -O2 -S race.c -o - | less    and find the loop — it is gone, replaced by a single add
Run it — the sanitizer names the racing line even though the count may look plausible
Optional: change the counter to _Atomic long, rebuild at -O0, and confirm the total is now exactly 1,600,000
blocks.expected: Five different wrong numbers, then a perfectly right number that is a lie, then the assembly showing why, then a tool that reports the bug regardless. That sequence is the most important thing in this module: you cannot test concurrency by running it and looking at the output.

blocks.title: The most useful thing in this lesson
blocks.text: In the verified run above, thread sanitizer reported the race and the program still printed exactly 1,600,000. The instrumentation slows execution enough that the threads rarely interleave — so the output looked perfect while the tool named the defect, the line, and the variable. Judge concurrent code by whether accesses are synchronised, never by whether the output looked right.

cheatsheet: counter++ is load, add, store — three steps, interruptible between any two
Measured: 8 threads x 200,000 increments reached 424,919 / 316,653 / 364,760 at -O0
At -O2 the same program printed exactly 1,600,000 — the optimiser collapsed the loop, hiding the bug
A right answer is not evidence of correct concurrent code
Race shapes: read-modify-write, check-then-act, lazy init, linked structures, file existence checks
volatile does NOT fix a race — it is about optimisation, not atomicity
gcc -fsanitize=thread finds races the run did not trigger
Thread sanitizer costs roughly 10x speed and cannot be combined with address sanitizer
Real fixes: a mutex, or an atomic type

checkpoint.prompt: Why can two threads each incrementing a counter 200,000 times end up far below 400,000?

choices.B: Each increment is load-add-store; interleaving makes two increments overwrite each other with the same value

checkpoint.explanation: Both threads read the same starting value and both write back the same result. One update is lost every time that interleaving occurs.

checkpoint.prompt: The same racy program prints the exactly correct total when built with -O2. What happened?

choices.B: The optimiser replaced the whole loop with a single add, so the window for interleaving nearly disappeared — the bug is unchanged
choices.D: The counter was cached in a register per thread

checkpoint.explanation: Verified in the generated assembly: the loop was replaced by one load, one add of 200,000, and one store. Correct output here is a property of the timing, not of the program.

checkpoint.prompt: Does declaring the shared counter volatile fix the race?

choices.B: No — volatile constrains compiler optimisation and reordering, but load-add-store is still three separate steps

checkpoint.explanation: This is one of the most common misconceptions in concurrent programming. Measured: with volatile at -O2, eight threads still lost about three-quarters of their increments. volatile is about how the compiler may transform accesses; atomicity requires a mutex or an atomic type. Verified: switching the same counter to _Atomic long produced exactly 1,600,000 on every run.

checkpoint.prompt: Your concurrent code passes 10,000 test runs. What have you established?

choices.B: Very little — a race with a narrow window can pass an enormous number of runs; use a tool that checks synchronisation rather than outcomes
choices.C: It is race-free on this hardware
choices.D: It is race-free at this optimisation level

checkpoint.explanation: That is what thread sanitizer is for: it reports unsynchronised access to shared data whether or not the run produced a wrong answer.
